questions.prompt: Put the stages that turn `prog.c` into an executable in order.
items: Linking the object files and libraries into the executable
questions.explain: `gcc prog.c -o prog` runs all three. `gcc -c prog.c` stops after compilation, producing `prog.o`.

questions.prompt: Which command compiles `a.c` to an object file without linking?
options: gcc a.c -o a
gcc -c a.c -o a.o
gcc -o a.o a.c -l
gcc -E a.c
questions.explain: `-c` means compile only. `-E` stops after the preprocessor; the first command also links.
option_notes: Compiles AND links into an executable.
Correct.
Malformed (`-l` needs a library name).
That only runs the preprocessor and prints the result.

questions.prompt: Who designed the C language, and while working on what?
questions.explain: C was designed by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs in the early 1970s, closely tied to the development of Unix (first on the PDP-11). C++ came later (Bjarne Stroustrup, 1980s) as an object-oriented extension of C.
options: Dennis Ritchie, at Bell Labs, while Unix was being developed
Bjarne Stroustrup, to add classes to Simula
Linus Torvalds, to write the Linux kernel
James Gosling, for set-top boxes at Sun
option_notes: Correct.
Stroustrup created C++, which builds on C.
Linux (1991) was written in C but C is much older.
Gosling designed Java.

questions.explain: C programs are compiled to machine code and stored in an executable. The language is imperative/structured (sequences of statements, functions) and, although high level, lets you work with addresses and bytes directly.
options: A compiled, imperative language that is high level but has low-level capabilities
An interpreted, object-oriented language that runs on a virtual machine
A purely functional language with garbage collection
A markup language that the operating system interprets
option_notes: Correct.
That describes Java-like languages: C has no virtual machine and no built-in objects.
C has no garbage collector: you free memory yourself.
C is a programming language, not a markup language.

questions.prompt: Match each build stage with what it does.
questions.explain: The preprocessor works on text (lines starting with `#`), the compiler turns each `.c` file into an object file, and the linker resolves the references between object files and libraries.
pairs: translates C source into machine code in an object file
joins object files and libraries into one executable

questions.prompt: Match each gcc command with the result it produces.
questions.explain: `-E` stops after the preprocessor, `-S` after compilation to assembly, `-c` after assembling to an object file; with none of them gcc also links.
pairs: the source after preprocessing, printed on the screen
an object file a.o, not linked

questions.prompt: To turn on the useful compiler warnings, add `{{0}}` and `-Wextra` to the gcc command.
questions.explain: `-Wall -Wextra` enable most warnings; most of them point at real bugs. `-Werror` makes warnings errors.

questions.prompt: Complete the command that compiles `main.c` with the C11 standard, debugging information and the output file `prog`.
questions.explain: `-std=c11` selects the language standard, `-g` adds debugging information (gdb, valgrind) and `-o prog` names the output file.
`#include` is a preprocessor directive: it pastes the header's text (declarations such as the prototype of `printf`). The code of `printf` itself is joined later by the linker.
options: The preprocessor copies the text of stdio.h into the program at that line
It links the whole C library into the executable
It runs stdio.h as a program before main
It imports a module, like `import` in other languages
option_notes: Correct.
Linking is a separate stage; the standard library is linked automatically.
A header contains declarations, not a program.
C has no module system: `#include` is textual copying.

questions.prompt: Which option selects the C11 language standard in gcc?
questions.explain: `-std=c11` (also `-std=c99`, `-std=c17`...). `-O` options are about optimisation and `-c` means compile only.
options: -std=c11
option_notes: Correct.
`-c` means compile without linking, and there is no `-c11`.
Options are case sensitive: this is not a gcc option.
`-O` is followed by an optimisation level such as `-O2`.

questions.prompt: What does the gcc option `-Os` do?
questions.explain: `-Os` is like `-O2` but avoids optimisations that grow the code, so it optimises for size (smaller code can also be friendlier to the cache). Note: a course slide describes it as 'cache efficiency'; the gcc manual says 'size'.
options: Optimises the generated code for size
Prints the operating system name
Adds debugging information
Optimises for speed at all costs
option_notes: Correct.
There is no such option.
Debugging information is `-g`.
That would be `-O3`/`-Ofast`.

questions.prompt: Sort these gcc options by what they control.
questions.explain: `-W…` options control warnings, `-O…` optimisation levels, `-std=` the language standard and `-g` the debugging information.
Execution starts at `main`, and there must be exactly one in the whole program (all files together). It can be anywhere in a file: only the declaration-before-use rule matters.
options: Every executable program has exactly one `main` function
`main` is where the program starts running
`main` must be the first function written in the file
Several `.c` files of one program can each define their own `main`
option_notes: True.
True.
False: functions may appear in any order as long as they are declared before use.
False: the linker would report a duplicate definition.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (Comments are not code.)
questions.explain: `//` comments out the rest of the line and `/* ... */` comments out everything up to `*/`, including line breaks. Only the first and last `printf` run.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? Mind the new lines.
questions.explain: The first `printf` ends with `\n`, so `mundo` starts on a new line; the second has no `\n`, so the output ends without a newline.
